source.title: Neural Networks-Based Equalizers for Coherent Optical Transmission: Caveats and Pitfalls
source.authors: Pedro J. Freire; A. Napoli; B. Spinnler; N. Costa; S. Turitsyn; J. Prilepsky

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own batch-size and generalization results for optical-channel equalizers, an application outside the image-classification and language settings named in V5.
record.gate_note: The paper reports batch-size effects on test Q-factor and training/test curves. Its random-label discussion cites prior work; it does not test fitting arbitrary labels alongside natural-label generalization. Other findings on PRBS memorization concern learning sequence-generation patterns, not random labels.
record.test_reason: The study measures generalization in optical-channel equalizers, which none of V1–V8 names. Its batch-size experiments concern optical MSE regression rather than V5's image classifiers or language models, and do not establish a matched fixed-epoch comparison. Random-label memorization and large-batch generalization findings are cited rather than replicated.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors identify periodic data, overfitting, misleading quality metrics, and complexity accounting as optical-equalizer pitfalls. Their regression equalizers generally improve with larger mini-batches up to saturation; regression outperforms classification in their tests, and L2 can improve constellation appearance without improving Q-factor. They explicitly describe their investigation as incomplete.
record.recipe_differences: Optical-channel equalization with MSE regression and Q-factor/MI measures; not the image-classification or language-model training setups in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Mini-batch size, modulation cardinality, equalizer architecture (MLP versus biLSTM), task (regression versus classification), training-data variability, PRBS order, and L2 regularization affect reported outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger batches generally improve held-out Q-factor for optical MLP and biLSTM MSE equalizers, with biLSTM gains saturating around batch size 1000. Some small-batch conditions produce distorted constellations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger mini-batches can improve optical-channel regression equalization, with effects depending on architecture and modulation.

fits_no_version.finding: The tested biLSTM regression equalizer has closely matching training/test curves and reaches 9.82 dB test Q-factor; the classifier overfits and reaches 7.74 dB. Their maximum test MI values are 5.97, a lower bound, and 5.87 bits/symbol, respectively.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: MSE regression generalizes better than categorical-cross-entropy classification in this optical equalization setup.

fits_no_version.finding: L2 regularization improves constellation appearance without matching large-batch performance; the separate MLP comparison yields 7.89 dB without L2 and 7.61 dB with L2.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Suppressing constellation distortion with L2 need not improve held-out optical equalization quality.

fits_no_version.finding: PRBS generation rules and repeated experimental traces can inflate apparent performance. Testing on another seed reduces one equalizer's Q-factor from 13 to 8.66 dB; training with diverse traces raises maximum independent-test Q-factor to 9.69 dB.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Periodic or insufficiently diverse optical training data can produce misleading generalization estimates.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Journal of Selected Topics in Quantum Electronics
record.problems: Results are specific to optical equalization and do not address the image or language settings of V5. Batch-size results are mostly Q-factor measures, and the text gives no uncertainty estimates. Table III reports values for selected batch sizes; detailed comparisons are also presented in figures. The authors state their conclusions are not exhaustive.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted due to the 60-row limit. Table III also reports batch sizes 16, 32, 64, and 128 for five modulation formats and both architectures; those intermediate numeric values were not extracted because rows already show the small-versus-large batch pattern across all listed modulation formats and architectures. Table III.

untested.parts: No paired natural-label and fixed-random-label fitting and held-out evaluation; learning PRBS structure is a different phenomenon.
No width sweep measuring test error beyond the zero-training-error threshold.
No convolutional-versus-fully-connected image comparison or local-connectivity intervention.
No adaptive-optimizer versus SGD comparison under specified tuning budgets.
No image-classification or language-model batch-size experiment, verified matched fixed-epoch comparison, or test of the specified adaptations.
No dropout intervention; L2 regularization alone does not test this version.
No magnitude-scaled weight-perturbation measure or ranking of generalization gaps. Gradient norms and weight distributions cannot substitute for it.
No influence-based selection and removal of memorized examples followed by retraining.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are relative to the supplied versions, so none-linked rows are cannot_determine even when their optical effects are measurable. Table III and Fig. 14 contain inconsistent small-batch biLSTM values; Section VII also misstates the 128-QAM comparison. These discrepancies do not establish a verdict on V5 outside its named workloads.

versions.untested_parts: Does not fit arbitrary labels or compare their held-out performance with natural labels.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
Uses Adam as a standard optimizer but does not compare optimizers.
Tests batch-size effects in optical equalizers, not the image-classification or language-model settings specified in this version.
Does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or compare generalization measures.
Does not remove memorized examples and retrain.
